titulo: The passive voice and «on»: When to use it, and alternatives

aula.objetivo: Form the passive voice with «être» + participle and «par», know when it is preferred, and use natural alternatives such as «on» and the pronominal form.

sessao.titulo: When to use it, and alternatives

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: in speech, use «on» when the agent is unspecified: «On parle français ici.» (instead of «Le français est parlé ici») STEP 2: use the pronominal form for things and habits: «Ça se dit.» «Le vin se vend ici.» «Ça ne se fait pas.» STEP 3: «se faire» + infinitive expresses that someone undergoes something: «Il s'est fait voler son portable.» (his phone got stolen) «Je me suis fait couper les cheveux.» (I had my hair cut) STEP 4: «se faire» is informal and very common; it avoids the passive in unlucky situations. STEP 5: «il paraît que» and «on dit que» attribute without giving a source: «On dit que ce film est excellent.» STEP 6: in the press, the passive highlights the fact: «Le président a été élu hier.» STEP 7: with «par», the agent appears; without «par», the focus is on the result: «Le magasin est fermé.» STEP 8: tenses: «est fermé» = state; «a été fermé» = action.
blocos.comparacao: in English we say «houses for sale» and «French is spoken here». French does the same with «on» and the pronominal form: «on parle français», «ça se vend». «Se faire» + infinitive (to have something happen to you) is very natural and has no direct equivalent: «se faire voler» is «to get robbed».

tabela.example: Il s'est fait voler son portable.

tabela.idea: to have something done by someone
